searchDocs.name: searchDocs
searchDocs.title: Search Dune Docs
searchDocs.description:
Natural-language query of the Dune docs at docs.dune.com. Calls the remote docs MCP search tool.

What this tool is for:
- Grounding answers in first-party Dune documentation.
- Looking up Dune-specific details on tables, datasets, SQL behavior, and API semantics.
- Pulling examples and canonical wording before composing queries or tool calls.

Usage tips:
- Start broad with query, then narrow using apiReferenceOnly or codeOnly.
- Pair with searchTables to move from concept to docs to table selection.

query.description: Natural-language query of the Dune docs. Example: 'decoded tables meaning', 'query pagination'.

apiReferenceOnly.description: If true, prioritize API reference pages over conceptual guides.

codeOnly.description: If true, prioritize pages with executable examples and snippets.

query.description: The normalized docs query that was sent to the remote search tool.

results.description: Ordered docs search results returned by the remote docs search tool. Each item is the parsed JSON value from a text block when JSON.parse succeeds, otherwise the raw text string.

searchTables.name: searchTables
searchTables.title: Search Tables
searchTables.description:
Natural-language table discovery across the Dune catalog. Required first step before writing, running, or executing any DuneSQL query — maps user intent into concrete table names so queries reference real tables instead of guessed names.

This is the best first tool when the user asks:
- What table should I use for X?
- Find me datasets for protocol Y.
- Show me tables for chain Z or topic T.

When to call this tool:
- Useful when you want to check Dune-specific details on tables and datasets.
- Useful when you need to move from vague intent to concrete table names.
- Useful when you need to find uploaded tables or transformation outputs.

Avoid this tool when:
- You already have a specific contract address and want decoded tables tied to it. Use searchTablesByContractAddress.

Fast usage patterns:
- Broad discovery: { "query": "uniswap volume", "limit": 20 }
- Curated-first: { "query": "dex swaps", "categories": ["spell"], "limit": 10 }
- Chain-constrained: { "query": "bridge transfers", "categories": ["decoded"], "blockchains": ["ethereum", "arbitrum"] }
- Uploaded tables: { "query": "*", "categories": ["community"], "datasetTypes": ["uploaded_table"] }
- Transformations: { "query": "retention cohort", "datasetTypes": ["transformation_table", "transformation_view"] }
- My private tables: { "query": "*" } - results include both public and private; use the "visibility" field in each result to distinguish them

Category semantics:
- canonical: base chain tables (transactions, blocks, logs, traces)
- decoded: ABI-decoded contract tables (events/calls)
- spell: curated Spellbook tables
- community: public community/uploaded tables

query.description: Natural-language intent or entity hints. Use protocol names, event/function names, or dataset intent. Example: 'uniswap v3 swaps'. Use '*' to browse without keyword bias.

categories.description: Precision filter for table families. Use ['spell'] for curated datasets; ['decoded'] for ABI-level events/calls; ['canonical'] for chain primitives; ['community'] for user-contributed datasets.

datasetTypes.description: Fine-grained dataset type filter. Use for uploaded tables and transformations.

blockchains.description: Chain scope to reduce ambiguity and improve ranking. Example: ['ethereum'], ['solana'].

schemas.description: Schema/namespace constraint for high precision. Example: ['dex'], ['uniswap_v3_ethereum'].

limit.description: Number of results per page. Use 5-15 for fast checks, 20-50 for deeper exploration.

offset.description: Pagination offset. Use previous response pagination.nextOffset for next page.

includeSchema.description: If true, include the column-level schema (name, type, nullable) for every result. Enable when preparing SQL generation.

includeMetadata.description:
If true, each result gains a metadata object with category-specific fields:
- All categories: page_rank_score (popularity signal, higher = more used), description (human-written summary).
- decoded tables: abi_type ("event" | "call"), contract_name (e.g. "UniswapV3Pool"), project_name (e.g. "uniswap_v3").
- spell tables: spell_type ("sector" | "project"), spell_metadata { depends_on: string[], tags: string[], description: string, columns: { column, name, description }[] }.
- uploaded/materialized_view: visibility ("private" | "public") is always included regardless of this flag.

total.description: Total number of matching tables across all pages.

full_name.description: Fully qualified table name to use in SQL, such as schema.table or namespace.table.

category.description: Top-level table family: canonical, decoded, spell, or community.

dataset_type.description: Fine-grained dataset classification such as dune_table, decoded_table, spell, uploaded_table, transformation_table, or transformation_view.

blockchains.description: Blockchains associated with the dataset when the catalog has that mapping.

partition_columns.description: Columns the table is partitioned by (e.g. ['block_date']). When writing SQL against this table, always include a WHERE filter on these columns to enable partition pruning and reduce query cost.

visibility.description: Visibility for datasets where it applies, especially uploaded or private tables.

description.description: Short human-readable dataset summary when available.

schema.description: Column-level schema keyed by column name when includeSchema=true. Use this to understand available fields before writing SQL.

metadata.description: Optional category-specific metadata returned when includeMetadata=true.

page_rank_score.description: Popularity or usage signal for ranking. Higher values generally indicate more commonly used tables.

description.description: Human-written summary of the dataset when available.

abi_type.description: Decoded-table subtype when available, typically "event" or "call".

contract_name.description: Contract name associated with a decoded table when available.

project_name.description: Protocol or project name associated with a decoded table when available.

spell_type.description: Spellbook subtype when available, typically "sector" or "project".

spell_metadata.description: Additional Spellbook metadata when available, such as dependencies, tags, descriptions, or documented columns.

results.description: Matching catalog entries ordered by the search backend relevance.

limit.description: The page size used for this response.

offset.description: The starting offset used for this response.

nextOffset.description: Offset to request the next page, or null when there are no more results.

hasMore.description: Whether additional results are available beyond this page.

pagination.description: Pagination state for continuing through additional result pages.

listBlockchains.name: listBlockchains
listBlockchains.title: List Blockchains
listBlockchains.description:
List indexed blockchain values with table counts, optionally filtered by category/query.

Best use cases:
- Before calling searchTables when chain names are uncertain.
- To detect multi-chain coverage for a topic/category.
- To decide whether a query plan should be cross-chain or chain-specific.

Typical flow:
- Step 1: call listBlockchains with categories and optional query.
- Step 2: pass selected chains into searchTables blockchains parameter.

Parameters:
- categories: Optional category pre-filter (canonical, decoded, spell, community).
- query: Optional semantic pre-filter before faceting. Use '*' for global counts.
- limit: Maximum number of blockchain values returned (default 200).
- offset: Offset for pagination.

categories.description: Category pre-filter. Example: ['decoded'] to list chains with decoded coverage.

query.description: Semantic pre-filter before faceting. Example: 'lending', 'nft'. Use '*' for global counts.

limit.description: Maximum number of blockchain values returned.

searchTablesByContractAddress.name: searchTablesByContractAddress
searchTablesByContractAddress.title: Search Tables by Contract Address
searchTablesByContractAddress.description:
Search for decoded tables associated with a specific contract address.

This tool finds all available decoded tables (events and calls) for a given smart contract address.

When to use this tool:
- You have a specific contract address (EVM or Tron) and want to find its decoded tables.
- You want to analyze on-chain activity for a particular smart contract.
- You need to find event or call tables for a known contract.

Avoid this tool when:
- You want to search tables by project name or keyword across categories. Use searchTables instead.
- You want broader table discovery across multiple categories. Use searchTables instead.

Decoded tables contain blockchain data that has been parsed according to a contract's ABI. They make it easier to analyze on-chain activity by providing a structured view of contract interactions.

Fast usage patterns:
- Find all tables for a contract: { "contractAddress": "0x..." }
- Filter by blockchain: { "contractAddress": "0x...", "blockchains": ["ethereum"] }
- Get schema for SQL: { "contractAddress": "0x...", "includeSchema": true }
- Pagination: { "contractAddress": "0x...", "limit": 20, "offset": 20 }

Table types:
- Event tables: contain parsed event logs emitted by smart contracts
- Call tables: contain parsed function calls made to smart contracts

createDuneQuery.name: createDuneQuery
createDuneQuery.title: Create Dune Query
createDuneQuery.description:
Create a new Dune query. Returns the query ID on success.

For brand-new analysis where the user wants the query executed, rows returned, or a visualization created, prefer createAndExecuteQuery instead. Use createDuneQuery directly when the user only wants to save SQL without running it.

Use this tool when the user wants to:
- Create a new SQL query on Dune
- Save a query they've been working on

**Important**: If the query targets tables with known partition columns (returned by searchTables or searchTablesByContractAddress), ensure the SQL includes a WHERE filter on those partition columns (e.g. `WHERE block_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7' DAY`). This enables partition pruning and significantly reduces query cost.

To save into a folder, use **folder_id** (after listDuneFolders, especially when the user names a parent path) or **folder_name** when the name is unique. If several folders share the same name, createDuneQuery returns **folder_ambiguous** with paths and ids—retry with **folder_id** or list with **parent_path** first. Do not pass both folder_id and folder_name.

Ownership is automatically derived from the authenticated API key's customer context.

name.description: Human-readable query title. Max 600 characters. Example: 'Daily DEX Volume on Ethereum'

folder_id.description: Optional folder ID to save the query into. Must belong to the authenticated user/team. Use listDuneFolders to discover ids, or use folder_name instead.

folder_name.description: Optional folder display name for this user/team (case-insensitive exact match on the folder basename). If multiple folders share this name, the tool errors with folder_ambiguous and lists paths and folder_ids—then pass folder_id or use listDuneFolders(parent_path). Do not set together with folder_id.

query.description: The SQL query text in DuneSQL dialect. Max 500,000 characters.

description.description: Short description of what the query does. Max 1,000 characters.

is_private.description: Whether the query should be private. Defaults to false. May be forced to true by team privacy settings.

is_temp.description: Whether the query should be temporary. Defaults to true for MCP-created queries. Temporary queries can be executed and they can have visualizations attached to them but they will not appear on the dune.com library and will not be accessible when shared with others. Set this to false if you intend to create a materialized view from this query (createMaterializedView rejects temporary queries).

parameters.description: Query parameters for parameterized queries. Each parameter includes key, type, value, and optional enumOptions.

key.description: Parameter name referenced in the SQL as {{key}}.

type.description: Parameter type. Use 'enum' with enumOptions to restrict values.

createAndExecuteQuery.name: createAndExecuteQuery
createAndExecuteQuery.title: Create And Execute Query
createAndExecuteQuery.description:
Create a new Dune query, execute it, optionally create a visualization, wait for results, and return the query, execution, visualization, and a result preview.

This is the default tool for brand-new SQL analysis requests where the user likely wants results. The model should still discover tables and write DuneSQL itself; this tool handles the deterministic Dune actions after SQL is ready.

Use this tool when the user wants to:
- Create and run a new Dune SQL query
- Create a new query and immediately inspect rows
- Create a new query and chart/table/counter together

Unless the user's question can be fully answered by inspecting raw result rows, provide a visualization. If the user asks for a specific visualization type, use that type; otherwise create a table visualization so the result is ready to render or add to a dashboard. The visualization object reuses generateVisualization's input shape without queryId.

Use lower-level tools for follow-up work:
- updateDuneQuery: fix SQL after an execution error or refine an existing query.
- executeQueryById: rerun an existing query.
- getExecutionResults: fetch more rows or a different slice from an existing execution.
- generateVisualization: add or change a visualization on an existing query.
- renderVisualization: render a returned visualizationId/queryId/executionId when the MCP client supports UI.

The result preview returns at most max_rows_returned rows from offset 0. If the execution is still running at timeout, the response returns the created query and execution, with result_preview showing the current pending/executing state and no rows.

Important: If the query targets tables with known partition columns (returned by searchTables or searchTablesByContractAddress), ensure the SQL includes a WHERE filter on those partition columns (e.g. `WHERE block_date >= CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '7' DAY`). This enables partition pruning and significantly reduces query cost.

chartType.description: Chart type to create. Must be one of: column, line, area, scatter, pie, counter, table.

tick_format.description: Numeral.js format for left y-axis tick labels (e.g. 0% or $0.0a). Omit for automatic formatting on create; on update, omitting keeps the current tick format — pass an empty string to reset to automatic.

title.description: Title shown on the left y-axis (e.g. 'USD volume', 'Transactions'). This is the axis label, not a series legend entry. Omit for no title on create; on update, omitting keeps the current title — pass an empty string to remove it.

getExecutionResults.name: getExecutionResults
getExecutionResults.title: Get Execution Results
getExecutionResults.description:
Get execution results for a query execution by execution ID.

This tool retrieves the results of a query execution. By default it waits for the execution to complete (up to the timeout) before returning results. While waiting, progress updates are streamed to keep the connection alive.

Behavior:
1. Checks the current execution status
2. If still running: polls until complete or timeout is reached
3. If completed: returns the result data
4. If failed/cancelled/expired: returns the error details
5. For completed executions, includes execution credit cost when available

When to use this tool:
- You have an execution ID and want to retrieve the query results
- You want to get the status of an execution

Response types:
- **Executing/Pending**: Execution is still in progress (returned only if timeout is reached or set to 0)
- **Completed**: Execution finished successfully with results
- **Failed**: Execution failed with an error message

Result shaping (optional, all combine):
- `outputColumns` — return only the named columns (saves bytes for charts).
- `orderByClauses` — raw SQL ORDER BY fragments, applied in order, e.g. `["\"block_time\" DESC", "\"hash\" ASC"]`. Quote column names that contain special characters.
- `sampleSize` — return a uniform random sample of N rows from the full result set. Incompatible with pagination — when set, the server returns a single response capped at N.
- `whereClause` — raw SQL WHERE expression to filter rows, e.g. `"\"block_number\" > 1000"`. Combine multiple predicates with AND/OR yourself.

**Important**: This tool can return up to 32000 rows per call (default 100). For very large result sets, consider:
- Save the query on https://dune.com to access full results through the web interface eg: "https://dune.com/queries/{query_id}"
- Or recommend using the Dune API directly for programmatic access to complete datasets.
  - Search docs for more SDKs or direct HTTP usage

Fast usage patterns:
- Wait for results (default): { "executionId": "01ABCD..." }
- Custom timeout: { "executionId": "01ABCD...", "timeout": 120 }
- Immediate check (no wait): { "executionId": "01ABCD...", "timeout": 0 }
- Get limited results: { "executionId": "01ABCD...", "limit": 50 }
- Project columns + sort: { "executionId": "01ABCD...", "outputColumns": ["time", "amount"], "orderByClauses": ["\"time\" DESC"] }
- Random sample for a chart: { "executionId": "01ABCD...", "sampleSize": 8000 }
- Filter rows: { "executionId": "01ABCD...", "whereClause": "\"amount\" > 0" }

Agent display instructions:
- If you render this data as a chart, table, or any other visualization for the user, include a "Powered by [Dune](https://dune.com/queries/{query_id})" attribution next to it, linking to the underlying query so the user can open it on Dune. Use the same query_id you passed to executeQueryById.

Create a query visualization and return both static and interactive chart URLs.

updateVisualization.title: Update Visualization
updateVisualization.description:
Update an existing visualization's name, chart type, and/or chart configuration.

Workflow: Use getVisualization first to inspect the current state, then call this tool with only the fields you want to change.

At least one of visualizationName or chartType + config must be provided. When updating chart type or config, both chartType and config must be provided together.

Important:
- The config parameter uses the LLM-friendly format (x_axis, y_axes, chart_type, etc.), not the raw Dune options returned by getVisualization.
- Build the config from scratch based on the query columns. Use getExecutionResults to inspect available columns.
- Column names in config must exactly match the query output.
- config.chart_type must match chartType.

Chart types: column, line, area, scatter, pie, counter, table.
Number formats (Numeral.js): 0, 0,0, 0,0.00, 0.0a, $0.0a (currency only), 0%.
Formatting: label_format formats tooltip and data-label values; tick_format / right_tick_format format the y-axis tick labels. Set both when the user asks for percentage or currency charts.
Duplicate x values: stacked charts keep only the first row per x value within a series by default — set when_duplicate_x 'sum' when the query can return several rows per x value. normalize_to_percentage renders each x value's series as shares of 100% (pair with tick_format '0%').
When the chart type stays the same, options not covered by the config (e.g. custom colors or UI-set tick formats the config omits) are preserved; changing the chart type rebuilds options from the config alone.
Grouped 2D charts: for long-form results such as date, protocol, volume_usd, put the category column in config.group_by_column and use one left y-axis value series.

Dual Y-axis: Only line and area charts support dual y-axis. Column and scatter charts require all series on the left axis.

Agent display instructions:
- If your client supports markdown images, render chartJpegUrl inline using markdown image syntax.
- Always include interactiveChartUrl as a clickable link so users can open and interact with the chart.
- If inline image rendering is not supported, provide both URLs as plain links.
- For private queries, the embed URL contains an API key. Treat those links as sensitive and do not share them outside the current user context.

getTableSize.name: getTableSize
getTableSize.title: Get Table Size
getTableSize.description:
Get the total storage size of a Dune table by analyzing its underlying physical tables.

This tool:
1. Runs EXPLAIN directly on QES to discover underlying physical tables
2. Queries size metadata for each underlying table
3. Aggregates and returns total size information

Use this tool when you need to:
- Understand the storage footprint of a table or view
- Debug query performance (larger tables = longer scans)
- Plan capacity or estimate costs
- Investigate which underlying tables a view references

Note: Views and spells (like dex.trades) may have multiple underlying tables - all are summed.

table_name.description: Fully qualified table name. Use "schema.table" for standard datasets (e.g., "ethereum.transactions", "dex.trades") or "dune.schema.table" for dune catalog datasets (e.g., "dune.stablecore.stablecoins_evm_activity_enriched").
The table name that was queried.

total_size_bytes.description: Total size in bytes across all underlying tables.

total_size_gb.description: Total size in GB across all underlying tables.

table_name.description: Full table reference from the query plan.

catalog.description: Catalog name if the table is qualified (e.g., "dune" for dune catalog datasets).

schema.description: Schema name extracted from the table.

size_bytes.description: Size in bytes if successfully retrieved.

size_gb.description: Size in GB if successfully retrieved.

error.description: Error message if size query failed.

underlying_tables.description: Details for each underlying physical table.

explain_execution_id.description: Execution ID used for the EXPLAIN execution.

createDashboard.name: createDashboard
createDashboard.title: Create Dashboard
createDashboard.description:
Create a Dune dashboard for blockchain and crypto data — covering DeFi, NFTs, DEX trading, token transfers, wallet activity, smart contract analytics, protocol metrics, gas fees, and any onchain data across Ethereum, Bitcoin, Solana, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, Optimism, and 20+ other chains.

Use this tool whenever a user wants to build a dashboard, report, or visualization page for onchain or blockchain-related data. Dune has indexed data from all major blockchains and protocols — if the data is onchain, Dune can query and visualize it.

This is the final assembly step that bundles queries and visualizations into a shareable dashboard. How you use it depends on what the user has already prepared:

Scenario 1: User asks to create a dashboard from scratch.
1. Understand the topic and break it into 3-6 logical sections.
2. Use searchTables and searchTablesByContractAddress to find relevant datasets. Use searchDocs if you need help with DuneSQL syntax or available functions.
3. Use createDuneQuery to build the section queries.
4. Execute each query with executeQueryById and validate the results with getExecutionResults.
5. Use generateVisualization to create charts for each query.
6. Call this tool with the resulting visualization IDs and any supporting text widgets.

Scenario 2: User already has queries and visualizations ready.
Collect the visualization IDs from previous generateVisualization calls and pass them directly to this tool. Add text widgets if the user wants headers or descriptions.

Scenario 3: User wants an empty dashboard to populate later.
Call this tool with just a name.

Tips for building great dashboards:
- Lead with a text widget containing a title and brief description.
- Group related visualizations together. The auto-layout places them in order.
- Use counter visualizations for key metrics at the top, then detailed charts below.
- Add text widgets between sections to provide context or explain methodology.

Agent display instructions:
- Present dashboardUrl as a clickable "Powered by [Dune](dashboardUrl)" link (use the dashboardUrl as the link target) so the user can open the full dashboard on Dune.

Update an existing Dune dashboard — change metadata, replace widgets, or both.

Use this tool to modify dashboards containing blockchain and crypto data — DeFi metrics, NFT analytics, DEX trading, token transfers, protocol dashboards, and any onchain data visualizations.

IMPORTANT: call getDashboard first. Widget updates use all-or-nothing replacement. When you provide visualizationWidgets, textWidgets, or paramWidgets, all existing widgets are replaced. To avoid losing widgets you want to keep:
1. Call getDashboard to fetch the current state.
2. Modify the fields you need.
3. Send the complete desired state to this tool.

All fields except dashboardId are optional. Only provided metadata fields are updated. Omitted metadata fields are preserved.

Widget replacement behavior:
- If none of visualizationWidgets, textWidgets, or paramWidgets is provided, existing widgets are preserved.
- If any of those widget fields is provided, the dashboard widget state is rebuilt from the supplied widget arrays.
- Widget types that are omitted during a widget update are cleared.

- Omit positions to auto-layout visualizations using columnsPerRow.

createMaterializedView.name: createMaterializedView
createMaterializedView.title: Create Materialized View
createMaterializedView.description:
Create a materialized view from an existing Dune query. Returns the matview ID, SQL table names, and the execution ID.

Use this tool when the user wants to:
- Materialize a query's results into a queryable table
- Create a scheduled refresh for a query's results

Important constraints:
- The source query must be saved as non-temporary (is_temp: false). Temporary queries cannot be materialized. Queries created via createDuneQuery default to temporary, so set is_temp: false there when you intend to materialize.
- The source query must NOT have parameters (parameterized queries cannot be materialized).
- Privacy is NOT settable here: a materialized view always inherits the privacy of its source query (public query → public matview, private query → private matview). To control a matview's privacy, set the source query's privacy. The returned is_private reflects this effective, inherited value.
- The source query must be owned by the same user/team that owns the materialized view, and must not be archived.
- The materialized view is owned by your authenticated context: in team context it is team-owned, in personal (user) context it is personal. To create a team-owned matview, authenticate in that team's context.
- The name must start with "result_", contain only lowercase letters, numbers, and underscores, be at least 8 characters, and not end with an underscore.
- The name is immutable after creation — it cannot be changed later.
- Performance tier ("small", "medium", or "large") is validated against the plan; availability depends on it ("small" is typically free-plan only, "medium"/"large" on paid plans). Larger tiers cost more compute.
- If a cron_expression is provided, it creates periodic refreshes. Use standard 5-part cron syntax. Minimum interval is 15 minutes.
- Creation triggers an immediate execution of the source query.
- Each query can have at most one materialized view. If one already exists for the given query_id, this call fails; use refreshMaterializedView to re-run it.

query_id.description: ID of the source query to materialize.

name.description: SQL-safe name for the materialized view. Must start with "result_", lowercase alphanumeric + underscores, min 8 chars, no trailing underscore. Example: "result_token_summary".

performance.description: Performance tier for the execution: "small", "medium", or "large". Availability depends on the plan ("small" is typically free-plan only); validated against it. Larger tiers cost more compute.

cron_expression.description: Cron schedule for periodic refresh (5-part cron syntax, e.g. "0 */6 * * *"). Minimum interval is 15 minutes. Null or omitted = no schedule.

expires_at.description: ISO 8601 datetime for schedule expiration. Null = no expiration.

matview_id.description: UUID of the created materialized view.

execution_id.description: Execution ID triggered by the creation.

is_private.description: Effective privacy of the materialized view. Always inherited from the source query's privacy; it cannot be set on the matview.

updateMaterializedView.name: updateMaterializedView
updateMaterializedView.title: Update Materialized View
updateMaterializedView.description:
Update an existing materialized view's settings. Returns the matview ID, SQL table names, and the execution ID.

Use this tool when the user wants to:
- Change the performance tier of an existing materialized view
- Add, change, or remove a periodic refresh schedule

Important constraints:
- The query must already have a materialized view (create one first with createMaterializedView). If it does not, the call fails.
- The matview is identified by query_id; you can obtain it from createMaterializedView or getMaterializedView output.
- The name cannot be changed — it is immutable after creation.
- Privacy is NOT settable here: a materialized view always inherits the privacy of its source query. To change a matview's privacy, change the source query's privacy. The returned is_private reflects this effective, inherited value.
- Performance tier ("small", "medium", or "large") is validated against the plan; availability depends on it ("small" is typically free-plan only). Larger tiers cost more compute.
- The update overwrites the refresh schedule, so pass the full intended state: cron_expression null/omitted removes any existing schedule, and expires_at null/omitted clears any existing expiration.
- Updating triggers an immediate re-execution of the source query.

query_id.description: ID of the query whose materialized view to update.

performance.description: Performance tier for the execution: "small", "medium", or "large". Availability depends on the plan ("small" is typically free-plan only); validated against it. Larger tiers cost more compute.

cron_expression.description: Cron schedule for periodic refresh (5-part cron syntax, e.g. "0 */6 * * *"). Minimum interval is 15 minutes. Null or omitted removes any existing schedule.

expires_at.description: ISO 8601 datetime for schedule expiration. Null = no expiration.

execution_id.description: Execution ID triggered by the update.

is_private.description: Effective privacy of the materialized view. Always inherited from the source query's privacy; it cannot be set on the matview.

getMaterializedView.name: getMaterializedView
getMaterializedView.title: Get Materialized View
getMaterializedView.description:
Fetch a materialized view by its fully-qualified SQL name.

Use this tool when the user wants to:
- Check the status or metadata of an existing materialized view
- Get the SQL table names to query a materialized view
- Verify ownership or privacy settings
- Check the table size of a materialized view

The name must be a fully-qualified SQL identifier in the format `dune.<team_or_user>.<name>` (e.g. `dune.my_team.result_token_summary`).

Authorization is enforced — only matviews visible to the requester are returned.

name.description: Fully-qualified SQL name of the materialized view (e.g. "dune.my_team.result_token_summary").

sql_names.description: Fully-qualified SQL table names for querying this materialized view.

is_private.description: Whether the materialized view is private.

table_size_bytes.description: Storage size of the materialized view in bytes.

last_execution_ids.description: IDs of recent executions that refreshed this materialized view.

deleteMaterializedView.name: deleteMaterializedView
deleteMaterializedView.title: Delete Materialized View
deleteMaterializedView.description:
Delete a materialized view. This permanently removes the materialized table and any associated refresh schedules.

Use this tool when the user wants to:
- Remove a materialized view they no longer need
- Clean up unused materialized views

This action is irreversible. The materialized view's SQL table names will no longer be queryable after deletion.
Only the owner (or team members with appropriate permissions) can delete a materialized view.

The name must be a fully-qualified SQL identifier (e.g. "dune.my_team.result_token_summary").

name.description: Fully-qualified SQL name of the materialized view to delete (e.g. "dune.my_team.result_token_summary").

listMaterializedViews.name: listMaterializedViews
listMaterializedViews.title: List Materialized Views
listMaterializedViews.description:
List materialized views owned by the authenticated user or team.

Use this tool when the user wants to:
- See all their materialized views
- Find a materialized view by browsing their list
- Check storage usage across materialized views

Returns a paginated list. Use limit and offset for pagination.

limit.description: Number of materialized views to return. Default 100, max 1000.

offset.description: Offset for pagination. Use next_offset from a previous response. Default 0.

is_private.description: Whether the materialized view is private.

next_offset.description: Offset for the next page, or null if no more results.

refreshMaterializedView.name: refreshMaterializedView
refreshMaterializedView.title: Refresh Materialized View
refreshMaterializedView.description:
Trigger a refresh of an existing materialized view. This re-executes the source query and updates the materialized table with fresh results.

Use this tool when the user wants to:
- Manually refresh a materialized view with the latest data
- Trigger an on-demand update outside of the scheduled cron

The name must be a fully-qualified SQL identifier (e.g. "dune.my_team.result_token_summary").
Only the owner (or team members with appropriate permissions) can refresh a materialized view.
The refresh consumes credits based on actual compute resources used.

name.description: Fully-qualified SQL name of the materialized view to refresh (e.g. "dune.my_team.result_token_summary").

performance.description: Performance tier for the refresh execution: "small", "medium", or "large". Defaults to "medium". Availability depends on the plan ("small" is typically free-plan only). Larger tiers cost more compute.

execution_id.description: Execution ID of the triggered refresh.

sql_names.description: Fully-qualified SQL table names of the refreshed materialized view.

renderVisualization.name: renderVisualization
renderVisualization.title: Render Visualization
renderVisualization.description:
Render a Dune visualization inside the MCP App.

For brand-new SQL analysis, prefer createAndExecuteQuery with visualization input first, then call renderVisualization with the returned visualizationId/queryId/executionId when the client supports UI rendering.

When called, the MCP client mounts the Dune visualization app (an interactive HTML
resource served at `ui://dune/visualization.html`). The app reads the input
arguments, fetches the visualization config via `getVisualization`, resolves
the execution to render (using `executionId` if supplied, otherwise the latest
successful execution for `queryId`), and pulls the data via
`getExecutionResults`. The app may also re-execute the query against
`queryId` if needed.

Use this tool when the user wants to *see* a chart, counter, or table rendered
in their client. For inspecting the underlying config or data without rendering,
prefer `getVisualization` / `getExecutionResults`.

visualizationId.description: The Dune visualization ID to render.

queryId.description: The query ID backing the visualization. The MCP App uses it to re-execute the query when no executionId is supplied or the latest execution is stale.

executionId.description: Optional execution ID to render. If omitted, the MCP App resolves the latest successful execution for the query.

visualizationId.description: The visualization ID forwarded to the MCP App.

queryId.description: The query ID forwarded to the MCP App.

executionId.description: The execution ID forwarded to the MCP App, when supplied by the caller.
